nameStory: This plant gets its "goosefoot" name from its distinctively shaped leaves that resemble the webbed foot of a goose. The "maple-leaved" part comes from the leaves' lobed shape that somewhat mimics a maple leaf, though they're much smaller and softer. It's also called "American" to distinguish it from its European cousin.
description: American maple-leaved goosefoot is an annual herb that grows 1-3 feet tall with a branching, somewhat sprawling habit. Its most distinctive feature is its soft, triangular leaves with pronounced lobes that give them a maple-like or goose-foot appearance. The plant produces tiny, inconspicuous greenish flowers clustered along the stems, followed by small seeds. It's a member of the same family as spinach and lamb's quarters, and has a similar weedy appearance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Triangular to diamond-shaped leaves with 3-5 pointed lobes, soft to the touch and somewhat succulent feeling. They're alternate on the stem and have a slightly dusty or mealy coating that rubs off on your fingers.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, greenish clusters without petals, arranged in dense spikes along the upper stems. They're easy to miss unless you look closely - just small, ball-like clusters that feel slightly rough.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright but often leaning or sprawling annual herb, typically 1-3 feet tall with multiple branching stems that feel somewhat fleshy and smooth.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dark, lens-shaped seeds enclosed in papery bracts. They fall easily when the plant is shaken and have a slightly shiny appearance.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Green to reddish, often with vertical ridges or grooves that you can feel when running your finger along it. The stem feels smooth and somewhat succulent.

habitat: Found in disturbed soils, waste places, gardens, and along roadsides throughout New England, though much less common than its weedy relatives. Prefers rich, nitrogen-rich soils and can tolerate some shade. Often grows near compost piles, farmyards, or areas where soil has been recently disturbed.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge in late spring with their characteristic lobed leaves already visible. Early leaves are often more deeply lobed and have a pronounced mealy coating.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full size and begin flowering in mid to late summer. The tiny flower clusters become most noticeable during this time as they develop along the upper stems.
seasonality.fall: Seeds ripen and scatter in early fall, and plants begin to turn yellow and die back. The dried seed clusters persist and rattle when shaken.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems may persist into early winter but eventually break down completely, leaving only seeds in the soil to germinate next spring.

funFact: Despite being called "American," this plant may actually be native to Europe and Asia - its true origins are debated by botanists, and it's so rare in New England (only 16 recorded observations!) that some scientists wonder if it's actually just visiting occasionally rather than truly established here.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with the much more common lamb's quarters, but lamb's quarters has simple, toothed leaves rather than the distinctive maple-like lobes. Remember: if the leaves look like tiny maple leaves, you've found the goosefoot; if they're just diamond-shaped with teeth, it's probably lamb's quarters.
contextualKnowledge: The goosefoot family has undergone major reclassification in recent years - this species used to be placed in the genus Chenopodium with lamb's quarters and spinach, but genetic studies moved it to its own genus. Don't be surprised if you see it listed under its old name Chenopodium simplex in older field guides.
compareHints: American maple-leaved goosefoot differs from its European relative (Eurasian maple-leaved goosefoot) mainly in leaf shape details and seed characteristics that require close examination. Within the broader goosefoot family in New England, it's distinguished from common lamb's quarters by its deeply lobed, maple-like leaves rather than simple diamond-shaped ones. The lobed leaves make it quite distinctive among our local goosefoot relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its close relative American maple-leaved goosefoot, the Eurasian species tends to have more deeply lobed leaves with sharper points and a more pronounced whitish coating on the leaf undersides.
